extracted.intended_audience: students and researchers in enumerative combinatorics (advanced undergraduate / graduate)
extracted.subtask_description: Solutions, sketches, and methodological guidance for a wide range of enumerative combinatorics exercises (compositions, partitions, permutations, generating functions, bijections, unimodality, q-series). The page illustrates proof techniques and counting strategies used to produce/verify combinatorial identities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Derive recurrences by case splitting on first part / membership
rubrics_metrics.description: Obtain counting recurrences by partitioning objects according to a simple combinatorial dichotomy (e.g., whether the first part is 1, 2, or ≥3, or whether a subset contains a particular element).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: in many parts (a)–(e) one considers whether the first part equals 1, 2, or ≥3 to derive Fibonacci-type recurrences; elsewhere decide for each i independently which T_j contains i to reduce to fk(1)^n. Use the natural disjoint decomposition of combinatorial classes to write Pn = P_{n-1} + P_{n-2} etc., then check initial conditions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Construct explicit bijective proofs (invertible maps)
rubrics_metrics.description: Prove equalities by giving an explicit, invertible mapping between the two combinatorial classes in question, and check uniqueness/invertibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Numerous examples: replace parts ai by constrained compositions to map compositions of n to compositions of 2n; mapping envelopes to increasing trees; bijections involving Ferrers diagrams and Frobenius notation; the sketch often requires checking that every target object arises exactly once and counting choices for local replacements (e.g., the 2^{ai-1} choices). When a bijection is unknown, the text notes that fact (e.g., 'A bijective proof is not known').

rubrics_metrics.name: Prove identities via generating functions and algebraic manipulation
rubrics_metrics.description: Translate combinatorial constructions into (ordinary or exponential) generating functions, manipulate algebraically (including substitutions), and extract coefficients to obtain counts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: deriving F_{2n} via identities like (x+2x^2+3x^3+...)^k expansions and rational-function manipulations; solve functional/differential equations arising from combinatorial decompositions (e.g., Riccati equation (1.154) for increasing binary trees); use coefficient extraction to relate generating functions to sequences (Fibonacci, Eulerian numbers, partition identities).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use factorization in free monoids for Fibonacci composition formulas
rubrics_metrics.description: Apply factorization techniques in free monoids to obtain composition formulas related to Fibonacci numbers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Gessel's systematic approach: model compositions by inserting at most one vertical bar among dots and circling one dot in each compartment; then translate bars/circled/uncircled dots into 1s and 2s to obtain bijections and counts (used to derive F_{2n} etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Replace parts by constrained local compositions and count multiplicities
rubrics_metrics.description: Build global bijections by replacing each part of a composition/partition with a local composition satisfying boundary constraints, and count the number of replacement choices per part.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: replace each ai by a composition αi of 2ai into 1s and 2s with αi beginning with 1, ending with 2, and internal constraints; each ai admits 2^{ai-1} replacements, leading to overall multiplicative counts. Always check that the global mapping is bijective and that counts multiply correctly.

rubrics_metrics.name: When bijections are unknown, provide (or prefer) generating-function proofs
rubrics_metrics.description: If no natural bijection is known, use generating-function methods as an alternative to prove enumerative identities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text explicitly notes when bijective proofs are unknown (e.g., some Knuth result) and presents generating-function verifications: show RHS satisfies recurrence and initial conditions or manipulate series identities to obtain coefficient formulas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use geometric/measure-preserving bijections (volume arguments) for permutation statistics
rubrics_metrics.description: Map regions (simplices) in Euclidean space measure-preservingly to count permutations with a given statistic (e.g., number of descents) by equating combinatorial counts to volumes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stanley's proof: define regions S_w in [0,1]^n corresponding to permutations, build a measure-preserving bijection ϕ to R^n_k so vol(S_{n,k}) = A(n,k)/n!. The bijection can be undefined on a measure-zero set but still valid up to measure zero.

rubrics_metrics.name: Apply analytic methods (differentiation, Rolle's theorem) and linear algebra for real-rootedness/unimodality/log-concavity
rubrics_metrics.description: Use calculus (differentiation, Rolle's theorem) and matrix/minor/linear-algebra arguments (Cauchy-Binet, nonnegative minors) to show real zeros, interlacing, unimodality, and log-concavity of coefficient sequences or polynomials.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: differentiate generating polynomials to obtain interlacing zeros; apply Rolle's theorem repeatedly to count simple negative real zeros; use Cauchy-Binet and properties of minors to deduce log-concavity and then unimodality; express products as nonnegative linear combinations of unimodal polynomials to conclude unimodality of products.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use the Principle of Inclusion-Exclusion (PIE) for counting with restrictions
rubrics_metrics.description: Employ PIE to count structures subject to exclusion constraints or to derive differential equations for generating functions when decomposing structures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cited in connection with Goulden & Jackson and used in derivations of functional/differential equations for tree enumerations and other constrained counts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use standardization maps to reduce multiset-permutation problems to permutation problems preserving statistics
rubrics_metrics.description: Apply the standardization (φ) that maps words/multiset permutations to ordinary permutations while preserving statistics like inv and maj, enabling the use of known permutation results.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: φ(w) standardizes a word to a permutation v with inv(w)=inv(v) and maj(w)=maj(v); thus equidistribution results for permutations transfer to multiset permutations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Verify closed-form expressions by checking recurrence + initial conditions
rubrics_metrics.description: Confirm a proposed closed-form/count by proving it satisfies the same recurrence and initial conditions as the combinatorial class being counted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used repeatedly: e.g., show RHS satisfies Fibonacci recurrence and base cases, then prefer a combinatorial proof if available. This is a valid verification strategy when a direct bijection is cumbersome or unknown.

rubrics_metrics.name: Count via cycle decompositions and logarithmic/exponential generating-function expansions
rubrics_metrics.description: Use cycle index / cycle decomposition techniques and expansions (e.g., log of generating functions) to enumerate permutations/cycles and multiset cycles; substitute equal variables for symmetric specializations when needed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: identity (1.155) expresses counts via sums over aperiodic cycles of given length; Lyndon/de Bruijn/Klarner/Gessel theories referenced; combinatorial verification by matching coefficients of expansions of log or exponential generating functions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Construct bijections using Ferrers diagrams and Frobenius notation for partitions
rubrics_metrics.description: Map lattice/path/walk structures to partitions by constructing the Ferrers diagram and taking Frobenius notation, enabling counting or bijective proofs between walks and partitions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: map concatenated spiral self-avoiding walks (CSSAW) to partitions via step-run lengths and Frobenius coordinates; the mapping yields explicit partitions (examples with figures given).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use substitutions and algebraic manipulation in q-series and modular identities
rubrics_metrics.description: Derive or transform q-series identities (Jacobi triple product, Rogers–Ramanujan, partition congruences) by making strategic substitutions and algebraic simplifications in product/sum forms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: substitute q^{1/2} or q^{3/2} into Jacobi triple product to obtain derived identities; use substitutions x→x^2, q→q x^{-1} into other identities; manipulate infinite products to derive partition congruences and combinatorial interpretations. The text references classical identities and how substitutions yield variants.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design insertion/iterative procedures to build structured partitions (e.g., lecture hall partitions)
rubrics_metrics.description: Define stepwise insertion rules (often starting from an empty or simple base object) to construct complex constrained partitions while maintaining the class constraints, thereby providing bijections or constructive proofs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: lecture hall partition construction by successive insertion of parts µ_i into λ_i with explicit local rules (add 1 to parts until certain conditions); verify the mapping is bijective by construction and example sequences provided.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use combinatorial/probabilistic intuition (e.g., Markov chains, carry processes) to explain distributions
rubrics_metrics.description: Apply probabilistic reasoning or Markov-chain viewpoints to obtain or explain combinatorial distributions (e.g., Eulerian numbers arising from carry probabilities).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Holte's and Diaconis–Fulman results: reason about carry probabilities in base-b additions to heuristically derive that the distribution of carries approximates Eulerian numbers; such intuition can be made rigorous and leads to enumerative interpretations.
